title: Kindness: Do It
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore the science of kindness, starting with animal altruism and Darwin's views on cooperation. They cover a Huddersfield University scale that groups kindness into benign tolerance, empathetic responsivity, and principled proaction; gender and age differences; the helper's high and oxytocin; a Hong Kong Polytechnic meta-analysis on prosocial behavior; studies on kindness to self versus others; how recipients benefit, including the ER visit study and the cupcake study; kindness in strong-tie relationships such as marriage, including the Gottmans' work on bids for attention; guilt and gratitude as motivators; compassion fatigue; and a listener mail about the NBA-ABA merger and the Saint Louis Spirit buyout.

segments.title: Show opening
segments.summary: Standard iHeart intro and hosts' introduction.

segments.title: Kindness in animals and Darwin
segments.summary: The hosts open on the mood the topic creates, then discuss animal altruism, the idea that kindness has a biological basis, and Darwin's emphasis on compassion and cooperation in communities.

segments.title: Kindness in children
segments.summary: Discussion of innate kindness in children, including the puppet and goldfish experiment and the Max Planck Institute study on toddlers' concern and relief when a grown-up needed help.

segments.title: Toddler study details
segments.summary: The hosts continue on the toddler research, with the Max Planck study tracking pupil dilation as a sign of concern.

segments.title: Measuring kindness: Huddersfield scale
segments.summary: A 2017 Huddersfield University scale grouped kindness into benign tolerance, empathetic responsivity, and principled proaction. Three shared traits define core kindness, and a set of unkindness questions was included. Gender and age differences are noted, along with a discussion of charitable giving across income levels.

segments.title: Charity and socioeconomic status
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether lower-income people give more relative to their means than wealthy donors, and the lesson of giving modeled to children.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Helper's high
segments.summary: The helper's high, first identified in the 1980s, is described as an exhilaration or calm after a kindness, which can be recalled later for similar feelings.

segments.title: Kindness as action and prosocial behavior
segments.summary: Kindness is defined as an action, with kindness.org calling it a meta value. Prosocial behavior research is applied to kindness.

segments.title: 2020 meta-analysis on prosocial behavior and eudaimonic well-being
segments.summary: A 2020 Hong Kong Polytechnic meta-analysis links prosocial behavior to eudaimonic well-being. Informal helping gives more personal benefit than formal giving. A detour follows on the word kindness as a noun.

segments.title: Surprise and kindness
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how surprise in spontaneous kindness adds to happiness, and a University of California study comparing acts of kindness with self-kindness, other activities, and art engagement.

segments.title: Kindness to self and the helper's high biology
segments.summary: A 2019 Oxford paper found kindness to others and to oneself had similar happiness effects. The helper's high is explained as a reward for exertion, linked to the vagus nerve and oxytocin.

segments.title: Oxytocin and the love hormone
segments.summary: Oxytocin is described as the love hormone, released in events like skin-to-skin contact and in acts of kindness.

segments.title: Witnessing kindness and mirror neurons
segments.summary: Witnessing an act of kindness may have a similar effect, possibly through mirror neurons, as cited in the Oxford research. Online kindness videos are discussed.

segments.title: Break lead-in
segments.summary: Transition toward how kindness benefits recipients. Short exchange on the term rascal scooter.

segments.title: Benefits for recipients: ER study
segments.summary: A 1995 study of unhoused ER patients found that those who received friendly student conversation rated their care higher and had a third fewer ER visits.

segments.title: Cupcake study and surprise
segments.summary: Eighty percent of participants gave away a cupcake. Recipients rated their happiness higher than givers expected, and surprise was cited as the cause.

segments.title: Kindness in family and newlywed studies
segments.summary: A 2017 study of newlyweds found kindness had the greatest effect when noticed and acknowledged. Strong-tie relationships can have less gratitude.

segments.title: Gottman research and bids for attention
segments.summary: John and Julie Gottman's research finds small acts of kindness matter in marriage, with a ratio of about four positive interactions to one negative. Bids for attention and turning toward are discussed.

segments.title: Personal anecdote on attention in marriage
segments.summary: Chuck shares his marriage experience and the value of paying attention.

segments.title: Guilt and gratitude as motivators
segments.summary: Guilt can drive kindness, but excessive guilt can exclude others. Gratitude can encourage generosity, even at a cost, and can be passed to third parties unconsciously.

segments.title: Pay it forward study
segments.summary: A 2006 study found that gratitude to a third party operated unconsciously, and conscious awareness reduced the effect.

segments.title: Pay it forward humor
segments.summary: Discussion of a Tim Robinson sketch about paying for the drive-through of the car behind.

segments.title: Compassion fatigue
segments.summary: Compassion fatigue is described for hospice nurses, single parents of high-needs children, and shelter workers, with symptoms including irritability and burnout. Self-care and resources are recommended. The hosts close by saying kindness is an action anyone can do.

segments.title: Closing thoughts on doing kindness
segments.summary: Kindness is an action that doesn't need cultivating, and the hosts suggest experimenting with it and charting the results.

segments.title: Listener mail: NBA-ABA merger and Saint Louis Spirit
segments.summary: Listener Steve from Seattle describes how ABA teams were bought out in the merger. The Silna brothers of the Saint Louis Spirit received about 800 million dollars total from the NBA for not operating a team.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and listener email information.
